JERUSALEM: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu boasted of his endorsement from Donald Trump on the eve of Israel's election, suggesting the two leaders could restart their war against Iran if he wins, after Trump said they should "finish the job". "US President Donald Trump has come with a friendship that has never existed before between an Israeli prime minister and an American president. And it is doubtful we will ever have such a friendly president again," Netanyahu said in a televised appearance late on Sunday (Oct 25) night. "He has another two years, and he says he is calling on you to vote for me." In his own social media post on Sunday, Trump, who launched the Iran war jointly with Netanyahu in February, said: "Vote for Bibi Netanyahu for Prime Minister, we have to finish the job that we started!" Netanyahu said Trump was willing to take action "that would finally, finally, remove the Iranian threat", but only as long as Netanyahu himself remains in power.

"And I have already instructed the Mossad and the IDF to bring down this regime, to bring down this regime because that is the only way to put an end to this threat," Netanyahu said, referring to Israel's main intelligence service and military. Asked for comment on Netanyahu 's remarks, White House Deputy Press Secretary Anna Kelly said: “As President Trump stated, Iran is in very bad condition, both economically and militarily, and the blockade will remain in full force and effect, with oil flowing in record numbers of barrels through the Hormuz Strait." "The United States will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections," Kelly added via email, referring to the Nov 3 vote in the US. Netanyahu's leading opponent, centrist former military Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, posted his own comments on social media, praising Trump as "a true friend of Israel". "I value his efforts and his commitment to Israel’s security, and I am confident that he will work in full cooperation with any leader chosen by the people."

Netanyahu says 'toppling' Iran government only way to end threat

EISENKOT ACCUSES NETANYAHU OF FEAR-MONGERING Tuesday's vote, Israel's first since the Oct 7, 2023, Hamas attacks, is the first chance for voters to deliver a verdict on the worst security failure in generations and the wars on multiple fronts that followed. With Netanyahu already at the helm of the most right-wing government in Israeli history, politics have shifted even further to the right. Nearly all Jewish-led parties, including that of the hawkish Eisenkot, now oppose the "two-state solution" that underpinned decades of peace negotiations with the Palestinians. But many voters say the divisive politics of Israel's longest-serving leader make the country weaker. Polls suggest Netanyahu's Likud Party will lose seats, potentially depriving his coalition of right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties of its narrow majority. Eisenkot and an array of opposition parties ranging from the rump of the centre-left to the right, also have no clear path to unseat him. Netanyahu, 77, is an unrivalled master of political survival: the only time since 2009 that opponents managed to wrest him briefly from the premiership, it took four inconclusive elections within two years to get him out. He was back 18 months later. Neither side planned major public events for Monday. But both posted on social media, drumming on the election's major themes — for Netanyahu, that he is the only leader with the mettle to face down Israel's enemies; for his opponents, that his divisive politics have weakened the country. Netanyahu shared an AI-generated video on Monday of Iran's Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, whose father Ali Khamenei was killed on the first night of US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February. Lying in a hospital bed, the younger Khamenei says his own vote would be "definitely not Bibi. Another term like this and I will be meeting my father sooner than expected". On Sunday, Netanyahu posted a computer-generated photo of a mushroom cloud over Tel Aviv, saying Israel was in existential danger from Iran. Eisenkot responded by accusing him of "relying on a campaign of fear-mongering, lies, and threats — including images of nuclear bombs in the heart of Tel Aviv. This time, it won’t work for him." Trump's endorsement of Netanyahu carries its own political risks a week before a legislative election in which his own Republicans are seeking to hold onto power. The Iran war is deeply unpopular in the United States, blamed for a surge in prices, especially for fuel. Major fighting has been suspended for months after ceasefire negotiations held without Israeli participation.

Source: Reuters/fh

PARIS, Oct 26 : Geoffroy Roux de Bezieux is expected to be named president of the organising committee for the 2030 Winter Olympic and Paralympic Games (OCOG) in the French Alps, a person familiar with the discussions told Reuters on Monday. Roux de Bezieux, the former boss of France's main business lobby MEDEF, is expected to be appointed at the organising committee's executive board meeting on Thursday. He would succeed Edgar Grospiron, who left the post last month before chief executive Vincent Roberti was appointed interim president. Roux de Bezieux, 64, had been named chair of OCOG's Remuneration Committee in April.

Oct 26 : Napoli coach Max Allegri has been handed a two-match ban for abusive remarks and an aggressive attitude towards match officials and an AS Roma staff member being sent off during Saturday's 3-3 home draw, Serie A's sports judge said on Monday. Allegri was dismissed shortly after Leonardo Balerdi scored a late equaliser for Roma. Allegri, who believed there was a foul during the build-up, reacted with anger when the VAR cleared the goal, leading to a straight red card. The manager, who has also been fined €10,000 ($11,200), is set to miss the Serie A games at Monza on Wednesday and Juventus on Sunday as his 10th-placed Napoli side look for a turnaround after winning only one of their last four league matches. Allegri made an "abusive remark towards the match officials" and later, in the changing room, "adopted an aggressive attitude towards an official of the opposing team," the disciplinary authority said in a decision published on the league's website.

Oct 26 : Anthropic unveiled its US initial public offering paperwork on Monday, setting up for a blockbuster market debut that would test investors' willingness to fund the AI juggernaut's bills amid growing worries over the massive debt-fueled spending. The company had submitted a confidential filing in June. In the recent weeks, exclusive reporting from Reuters highlighted its sweeping AI ambitions, mounting costs and concerns about the "existential risks to humanity" that advanced AI poses. Here are a few details on Anthropic's financials, business structure, and where it stands in the global AI race: BACKGROUND AND FINANCES

Founded in 2021 by former OpenAI researchers including siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, Anthropic is the startup behind the Claude family of AI models. Across four tiers - Fable, Opus, Sonnet and Haiku - Claude powers products such as Anthropic's chatbot, coding agent and the enterprise-focused Claude Cowork AI agent. Anthropic's early focus on training its models for coding tasks propelled the company to the forefront of the AI race and helped it draw a steady stream of enterprise customers. A majority of its revenue comes from businesses paying for its models per use, measured in "tokens" of information processed, in what Anthropic calls "consumption-based" revenue. It also generates revenue from its paid customer subscription tiers such as "Pro" and "Max". That has helped Anthropic grow its revenue to $4.59 billion in 2025 from $386 million a year ago and $41 million in 2023. For the six months ended June 2026, Anthropic's revenue was $16.29 billion. But the rapid growth is accompanied by bigger losses. Its operating loss for the first half of 2026 was $693 million. In 2025, it was $8.06 billion, up from $2.98 billion a year ago. COSTS, COMPUTE DEMAND AND CIRCULAR AI INVESTMENTS Computing power is Anthropic's biggest expense. The company's costs include computing fees paid to cloud services providers such as Amazon Web Services and Google Cloud, costs tied to data center facilities and renting data center capacity, equipment leases and energy bills. Over the past three years, Anthropic's compute and infrastructure expenses have dwarfed its revenue. The company has committed more than $500 billion in spending with six partners over a decade - one of the largest AI buildout commitments on record. Anthropic said many portions of its agreements are non-cancelable or require payments regardless of usage. It has committed to spend at least $110 billion with Amazon, about $114.5 billion with Google and $44.9 billion with Microsoft for cloud computing over the next seven to 10 years. But some of those companies are also its largest backers. Amazon and Google are among Anthropic's top shareholders, marking yet another example of the circular financing structures that have dominated capital flows in the AI industry. Amazon has invested at least $13 billion in Anthropic and has agreed to invest up to $20 billion more. Google has committed up to $40 billion to Anthropic. GOVERNANCE AND STRUCTURE Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, or PBC, meaning it is legally obligated to balance profitability goals for investors with developing AI for the benefit of humanity. An independent body elects a majority of its board. The company, helmed by Dario Amodei as CEO and his sister Daniela, as president and chair of the board, will continue to operate as a PBC after its listing. It expects to keep its founders and an independent trust in control, in a structure that could limit investor oversight and public shareholders' influence. The company has said it needs to concentrate control and capital in fewer hands to reduce AI's risks. Under this arrangement, a majority vote of its seven co-founders will direct a single share of Class F stock that amounts to 50.1 per cent of the total voting power over key corporate matters, including the election of some board directors and other matters submitted to investors. COMPETITION Anthropic's most direct competitor is OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, whose 2022 launch kick-started the global race to advance and adopt AI technologies. Following Anthropic's lead in the enterprise market, OpenAI has also sharpened its focus on products for developers and business customers. Anthropic is also locked in a race with Elon Musk's SpaceX and Alphabet's Google. All of them are spending billions of dollars into model development, data centers and specialized AI chips as they vie for dominance in generative AI. Ramp data, which captures a slice of AI spending by business customers, showed Anthropic accounted for 60.1 per cent of AI token spending in the week ended October 11. The startup has gained ground against rivals increase spending on AI services.

Source: Reuters

CAPE TOWN, Oct 26 : Australia will give key batter Steve Smith as much time as possible to prove his fitness ahead of the third and final test against South Africa at Newlands, captain Pat Cummins said on Monday. Smith injured his neck in South Africa’s innings and 31-run victory in the second test in Gqeberha which levelled the series at 1-1 going into the decider in Cape Town starting on Tuesday. "Hopefully, it all goes well and he'll be there," Cummins told reporters on Monday. "But we just want to wait for that last piece of the puzzle (before naming a team). Cummins said Cameron Green would bat “preferably in the middle order”, which will likely mean Matt Renshaw opening with Travis Head after Nic Maddinson was dropped from the squad.

For Smith, it would be a return to the scene of his darkest day after his role as captain in the "Sandpapergate" scandal that rocked Australian cricket in 2018. “He's been awesome this tour," Cummins said. “In the last couple of years, probably particularly the last 12 months, it feels like he's in a really good place and he's enjoying his cricket. “He’s getting himself out (and about), whether it is playing golf or going for coffee club every morning. He's been super invested in what's going on and very helpful for me out in the middle." Smith has averaged a little over 20 in four innings with the bat and took a blow to the head in the first test, before injuring his neck in the second. “He looks in total control of how he's going about his work. He's one of the greatest batters we've ever had. You don't play 100 odd tests without matches where you're not 100 per cent fit," Cummins said. Cummins was part of the side involved in the Sandpapergate scandal, though denies any knowledge of events, and another infamous test Australia played in Cape Town in 2011. "My first ever test experience was here. I was running the drinks and we got bowled out for 47. So that was a wild introduction," he said with a smile.

Source: Reuters

Oct 26 : Anthropic disclosed steep losses and red-hot revenue growth in its US IPO filing on Monday, as the Claude-parent laid out its ambition to build AI systems capable of reshaping the global economy despite the high costs of developing the technology. The prospectus highlights the AI company's rapid growth over the past year, fueled by Big Tech's breakneck spending that has driven a rally in AI stocks while raising concerns about lofty valuations and rising debt. The company also flagged growing risks from AI technology, underscoring concerns over its potential to cause harm which had led CEO Dario Amodei to call for a slowdown in development of advanced models. Anthropic's net loss in the first half of 2026 widened sharply to $80.7 billion, largely due to a rise in the fair value of bonds convertible into company's shares. Revenue in this period stood at about $16.3 billion.

The company's revenue grew a staggering 1,368 per cent in the three months ended June 30 from a year ago, but warned in the prospectus that revenue growth rate could decline over time and fluctuate from time to time. The IPO, which is likely to be as early as later this month, is expected to establish Anthropic, the AI lab behind the viral Claude models, as a benchmark for how Wall Street values leading AI companies, including rival OpenAI. The IPO push comes despite a once-busy fall listing calendar thinning out as choppy markets prompt companies to delay their offerings. Analysts said that would give Anthropic access to a deep pool of capital to fund its costly AI ambitions. Growing investor uneasy with the debt-fueled AI investment boom has led to a global selloff in AI and tech stocks as they start to doubt if the trillions spent on data centers, chips and computing capacity will generate fast returns to support lofty valuations. Higher borrowing costs and rising bond yields have added to their caution. However, tech companies are still hungry for cash. Meta is aiming to raise up to $95 billion in its largest-ever equity fundraising, while SpaceX has inked a $40 billion deal with Apollo to lease AI chips and server hardware. VALUATION EXPECTATIONS Some current and prospective investors are valuing Anthropic at about $1.5 trillion, down from roughly $2 trillion a week ago, after the AI startup disclosed some financial details at a recent investor event, Reuters reported. "While Anthropic is well-capitalized, an IPO would give the company some valuable financial flexibility. No company wants to spend too long on the cusp of going public, since that can be a distraction," said Matt Kennedy, senior strategist at Renaissance Capital, a provider of IPO-focused research and ETFs "Maybe they could have gotten a higher valuation next year, but they've decided to "rip the band-aid off". The filing confirmed a series of Reuters exclusives that offered an early peek at its contents before Anthropic made it public, including details of its financial performance, growth trajectory and IPO plans. BALANCING AI'S PROMISES AND PERILS Anthropic said more than half of Fortune 500 companies and over 30 per cent of Global 2000 firms were customers generating at least $100,000 each in revenue for the company over the 12 months ended September 30. The IPO comes as Anthropic's own research raises concerns about advanced AI systems, which in controlled tests have shown behaviors including code sabotage, fraud assistance and information manipulation. The findings have fueled concerns about how companies can keep powerful AI systems under control as they race to deploy them commercially. The prospectus also highlighted risks associated with its AI models, which it said could exhibit "self-preserving behaviors", including behavior "resembling blackmail". "Our increasing use of AI systems to accelerate our own research and development may cause the capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement corresponding safety, alignment, and security measures," it said. The company said it relies on a limited number of cloud services providers such as Amazon, Google and Microsoft and suppliers such as Broadcom for compute and critical parts of its infrastructure These relationships can create "dependencies and potential vulnerabilities", it said. Anthropic will trade on the Nasdaq after the IPO closes under the ticker symbol "ANT".  The filing did not reveal the terms of its offering, including the number of shares it plans to sell and the proposed price range. RED HOT GROWTH Anthropic, founded in 2021 by a team of researchers, was valued at $965 billion in May in a funding round that drew some of the biggest names in Silicon Valley and Wall Street. Amazon and Google were among Anthropic's early strategic partners, investing billions of dollars in the startup while providing the cloud infrastructure needed to train and deploy Claude models. "We believe this abundance of AI will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors and the internet," the prospectus said.  The company said it expects compute and infrastructure expenses to increase in absolute dollars and remain its largest operating expense for the foreseeable future. Anthropic remains locked in a fierce battle with OpenAI to lead the race to build the most advanced AI systems. The ChatGPT maker confidentially filed for an IPO in June and is expected to list by early 2027. Anthropic's IPO follows that of Elon Musk's SpaceX, which rewrote the IPO record books in June, when it priced a $75 billion offering that valued the company at $1.75 trillion. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley were named as the lead banks for the IPO alongside 20 others as underwriters. Morgan Stanley will act as a stabilization agent, overseeing the stock's early trading. The roles mark another major win for Goldman and Morgan Stanley as they had led SpaceX's IPO too.

Source: Reuters

SAN FRANCISCO, Oct 26 : Cadence Design Systems on Monday launched a portfolio of AI models tuned to help design computer chips, deepening its partnership with Nvidia and diverging from rival Synopsys's recent deal with OpenAI. Both companies make software used to design computing chips — a process that involves arranging billions of transistors precisely to meet cost and performance targets — and are racing to have AI "agents" use those tools on behalf of human engineers to speed up the process. The new suite, called Cadence Maestro, introduced on Monday, was built in part on Nvidia's open-weight Nemotron model and secured with Nvidia's OpenShell safety technology, the companies said. Cadence said customers can run the models on its own cloud or any public cloud, or keep them entirely in-house behind their own firewalls and data centers.

The plan focuses on five measures to remedy the breach, and Temu now has four months to conduct an interim risk assessment, the Commission, which acts as EU regulator, said in a statement. Temu, along with Shein and other ecommerce platforms, has been hit by the EU imposing €3 fees on low-value ecommerce packages since the start of July. Bonds of Nebius maturing in 2034 and those of CoreWeave expiring in 2033 have hit record lows on the concerns. Saudi Arabia's main international airport in Riyadh has become a repeated target of attacks by Yemen's Houthi rebels, disrupting flights and raising concerns about the security of civilian aviation in the kingdom. On Monday (Oct 26), the Saudi-led military coalition said it had intercepted a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis towards Riyadh, after the Iran-backed group claimed another attack on King Khalid International Airport. The latest incident came as flights resumed at the airport following weeks of disruption, with the Houthis warning airlines and travellers that the facility remained "unsafe" and a "military target". But the Houthis' attacks on Saudi airports are not new. As far back as November 2017, the group fired a ballistic missile towards King Khalid International Airport, which Saudi authorities said they intercepted.

In June 2019, a missile struck Abha International Airport in southern Saudi Arabia, injuring 26 civilians. The latest escalation has been particularly deadly. Earlier this month, an attack on Riyadh airport killed 13 people and wounded more than 300 , marking the deadliest such incident in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade. The attacks have disrupted travel plans for thousands of passengers, forced the postponement of Saudi Arabia's flagship investment conference until 2027 and cast uncertainty over the kingdom's ambitions to become a global tourism and business hub . CNA looks at why the Houthis are repeatedly targeting Saudi civilian infrastructure, and what this means for travel in the Middle East.

Houthi activists stand on a platform against a banner depicting Houthi missiles at an anti-Saudi rally amid an escalation with the kingdom, in Sanaa, Yemen on Jul 31, 2026. (File photo: Reuters/Khaled Abdullah)

Why are the Houthis targeting airports? Airports are among a country's most strategically and economically important infrastructure, making them particularly disruptive targets during a conflict. The Houthis' raids on Saudi airports are part of a wider series of attacks on the kingdom's infrastructure, including on oil tankers and pumping stations. Missiles have also been fired towards the Saudi cities of Taif and Yanbu. The latter is a major oil export hub on the Red Sea coast that has allowed Riyadh to bypass Iran's blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. The Houthis have described Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport as a military target and warned airlines against using it. However, the group's claims do not by themselves establish that the airport is a lawful military target under international humanitarian law. United Nations secretary-general António Guterres has called for an immediate halt to attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, saying that they violate international law.  Besides Riyadh, airports in Abha, Dammam, Najran and Jizan have also come under attack. The Houthis' targeting of critical infrastructure bears similarities to tactics used by their main backer, Iran, which has also launched attacks on infrastructure across Gulf Arab states.

Related:

Flights resume at Riyadh airport as Houthis attack Saudi Arabia

CNA Explains: How the Houthis could threaten the Red Sea and shape the Iran war

What triggered the latest escalation? The conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis dates back to 2015, when Riyadh led a military intervention in Yemen against the Iran-backed group. A United Nations-brokered truce in April 2022 brought a significant reduction in hostilities, including cross-border attacks. Although the ceasefire formally expired six months later, a relative calm largely held. Tensions flared again in July 2026 when the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of launching airstrikes on Sanaa International Airport in Yemen's capital. Yemen's internationally recognised government's defence ministry said the strikes were intended to prevent an Iranian aircraft from landing at the airport. The Houthis subsequently launched missile and drone attacks on Abha International Airport, with no casualties reported. The group also declared a maritime blockade of Saudi Arabia and began targeting its ships, territory and oil facilities, before launching a major offensive in September in which they seized Yemeni government-held territory along the Red Sea coast. The Houthis have also reported frequent Saudi airstrikes on areas under their control.

What impact are these attacks having on Saudi Arabia? The Houthi attacks have severely disrupted Saudi Arabia's aviation sector, forcing Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport to close for two weeks before resuming operations on Sunday (Oct 25). The fallout has extended beyond aviation, with several major international events cancelled, postponed or relocated over security concerns. Saudi Arabia has postponed its flagship Future Investment Initiative conference until 2027, while organisers of the prestigious motor sport race Dakar Rally on Sunday said it would move to a different location.  Golf's Asian Tour postponed the Saudi International indefinitely and cycling's Urban World Championships was cancelled earlier this month, while the tennis tournament Six Kings Slam was postponed to December. These disruptions come as Saudi Arabia pursues its Vision 2030 plan to diversify its economy.  Prolonged instability could undermine investor confidence and make it harder for it to attract international visitors, businesses and major events. The country's energy infrastructure has also come under threat. In September, Saudi Arabia temporarily shut down its 1,200km East-West pipeline as a precaution after a drone attack that Riyadh and Baghdad said originated in Iraq. The pipeline has served as a key route for Middle East oil exports amid the war-related disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. On Oct 24, the Houthis claimed to have targeted the pipeline, crude oil pumping stations, an Aramco facility in Yanbu and the Rabigh refinery. Saudi Arabia has not confirmed those claims.

Related:

US orders diplomats to depart Saudi Arabia amid Houthi strikes

Saudi says intercepted Houthi missile, blasts heard in capital

What is the official advice about travelling to Saudi Arabia? Amid the escalating violence, the United States has ordered some diplomats and their family members to leave its missions in Saudi Arabia , and plans to withdraw family members from several other US missions in the region. Washington had returned some diplomatic personnel to the region in recent months, after many were pulled out following Iranian attacks on US facilities when the US-Israeli war against Iran began in late February. On Singapore's part, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs has advised Singaporeans to defer all travel to Saudi Arabia , citing an increase in missile and drone attacks targeting civilian aviation and energy infrastructure. The Islamic Religious Council of Singapore (MUIS) has also advised Singaporeans planning to perform Umrah to consider postponing their trips to Saudi Arabia . Umrah is a voluntary pilgrimage to Mecca that Muslims can undertake at any time of the year. Despite the advisories, some Singaporeans are pressing ahead with their pilgrimage plans. Some families CNA spoke to earlier this month said that they were adopting adopt a " wait-and-see” approach, while others have had their pilgrimage cancelled.

Related:

Some Singapore pilgrims press ahead with Umrah plans despite advisory, others face cancellations

Singaporeans advised to defer all travel to Saudi Arabia amid heightened security risks: MFA

Singapore condemns Houthi attacks on civilian aviation infrastructure in Saudi Arabia

Why are the Houthis able to strike Riyadh so often? Iran has provided the Houthis with weapons, funding and training for more than a decade, although Tehran denies arming the group in violation of a United Nations arms embargo. Despite Iran facing its own financial and military strains due to war and sanctions, the Houthis have learned - with Iranian help - how to assemble their own weapons, including drones and missiles, experts interviewed by Reuters said. Iran's Revolutionary Guards and members of Iran's other ally, Lebanese Hezbollah, initially gave the Houthis knowledge of missile systems and their operation, Andreas Krieg, senior security studies lecturer at King's College London told Reuters. "Former Yemeni military engineers and a growing generation of locally trained specialists have helped institutionalise these capabilities," he said. "Tehran has not simply supplied the Houthis with weapons. It has helped create an indigenous military-industrial learning process that becomes progressively harder to dismantle, even if direct Iranian supply routes are disrupted." This has made the Houthis one of Iran's most cost-effective and valuable regional military allies. The group has also reportedly turned to artificial intelligence to enhance its weapons capabilities. Anthropic said last month that "a cell of threat actors based in northern Yemen" had used its Claude AI assistant to help develop software for a guided rocket, a planned ballistic missile with a range of more than 2,000km and a missile variant incorporating a hypersonic glide vehicle. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia's air defences face mounting pressure from repeated missile and drone attacks, even as its US ally grapples with demands on its own air defence resources amid the war with Iran.

Source: CNA/Agencies/nh

FRANKFURT, Oct 26 : AI is helping Deutsche Bank cut decisions for some smaller corporate lending from weeks to just minutes, its new technology chief Marie-Jeanne Deverdun told Reuters. The project, which went live in the summer, also reduces the time taken to make some lending decisions for multinational corporations from months to weeks, said Deverdun, who joined Deutsche Bank's management board this year. "For smaller corporates, which are less complicated in their setup and their legal structure, we're talking weeks to minutes," Deverdun said in an interview. Deverdun said Deutsche Bank is also preparing for a future when its AI agents will interact directly with clients' own agents, as lenders are drawn into the debate among technology leaders over whether AI development is moving too fast.

"We are watching that debate carefully. These are very valid concerns, and, obviously, the management of cyber risk is my number one priority," she said. "We're spending a lot of resources and budget to continue to protect the bank from those new technologies and threats," she added. Banking regulators are stepping up efforts to contain growing AI risk as lenders race to deploy the technology while balancing questions over returns and security threats. Deutsche Bank, Germany's largest lender, plans more than €2.5 billion ($2.80 billion) in tech spending between 2026 and 2028. By comparison, JPMorgan is budgeting $20 billion for 2026. Banks hope AI will trim costs and boost productivity. Britain's Barclays said last week it was cutting around 5,000 jobs or 5 per cent of its workforce this year as it uses the technology. Citigroup has said AI was now developing products at lower cost and up to 40 per cent faster. Major US banks, meanwhile, have begun blocking third-party AI agents from operating inside customer accounts in response to concerns that sophisticated AI agents could harm the banking system and the institutions trusted to hold people's wealth. Deutsche Bank CEO Christian Sewing has said he wants to make Deutsche "a truly AI-powered bank" after his predecessor said in 2015 its systems were "disjointed, cumbersome and far too often just plain incompatible". After the Ukraine war began, Deutsche Bank had to move its tech staff out of Russia and it is still streamlining an array of platforms, although it has cited some recent progress. Deverdun said Deutsche Bank had built an internal AI platform known as ADA, named after computing pioneer Ada Lovelace, to develop, monitor and control AI agents. ADA allows the bank to oversee agent activity, manage risk and switch between AI models as technology evolves, she said. "We're already preparing for an agentic economy where our agents interact with the agents of our clients with clear accountability and the right controls," she added. ($1 = 0.8937 euros)

Oct 26 : Meta Platforms said on Monday it plans to raise up to $95 billion in its largest-ever equity fundraising, as the social media giant spends aggressively on its AI infrastructure expansion. The Facebook parent has launched public offerings worth about $35 billion in common and preferred stock, and said it also plans to launch a separate at-the-market share sale program worth up to $60 billion. The company will launch the larger share sale program after its new non-voting Class C shares begin trading, which is expected in the first quarter of 2027, but said it has not yet finalized its timing and terms of the sale. Meta's fundraising plan, among the biggest by an AI company, has also drawn interest of up to $5 billion in total from Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom for Class A shares.

Their funding interest adds to concerns about an increasingly circular flow of capital in the AI industry, as chip suppliers help finance the expansion of one of their biggest customers. Meta has been pouring money into chips and data centers to compete better with OpenAI and Anthropic. "We expect investors to continue to question the financing and potential for future capital raises," William Blair analysts said in a note. "Overall, we believe the financing reinforces both Meta's confidence in the long-term returns from AI investment and the increasingly capital-intensive nature of pursuing that opportunity." The company's shares fell about 1.4 per cent in morning trading. The latest fundraising further underscores a shift among big technology companies increasingly tapping debt markets and raising equity to bolster their AI infrastructure, having previously relied on cash to fund their investments. Earlier this year, Alphabet increased the size of its equity offerings to $84.75 billion. Separately on Monday, SpaceX said an affiliate of Apollo Global Management will buy AI chips and server hardware and lease them to the rockets-to-AI firm, in a deal with total principal payments of about $40 billion. META'S AI SPENDING IS BURNING CASH Meta has committed to spend about $825 billion in the future, primarily driven by its growing investments in data centers, AI-related infrastructure and cloud computing power. But the aggressive expansion has eroded its historically strong free cash flow. The company reported a $2.12 billion cash burn in the third quarter, its first negative free cash flow in over a decade, compared with a positive cash flow of $10.63 billion a year ago. Still, the early popularity of its consumer-focused AI agent Muse and release of a competitive new series of AI models have helped partly justify Meta's aggressive investments. "We believe that Meta will ultimately produce a profitable AI business and its returns longer-term should help the company diversify, although the path may not be linear," William Blair analysts said. The company had cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities of $82.45 billion and long-term debt of $80.92 billion as of September 30, according to its latest quarterly filing. Last week, Meta raised the lower end of its annual capital expenditure forecast to a range of $135 billion to $145 billion. The company has said it would issue Class C common stock in January 2027, effectively resulting in a two-for-one split, to fund acquisitions and retain top talent while maintaining CEO Mark Zuckerberg's control. Meta agreed to grant Zuckerberg Class C shares that he can sell to help pay a potential California billionaire wealth tax, in exchange for a commitment to keep him in California.

Source: Reuters
